Abstract The selection of cadence during cycling may be determined by a number of factors, including the degree of oxygenation in the exercising skeletal muscle. The purpose of this study was to determine the degree of muscle oxygenation associated with different cycling cadences and exercise intensities, and its putative role in the choice of self‐selected cadence during cycling. We recorded cardiopulmonary and metabolic responses to cycling at exercise intensities of 70% and 90% of the ventilatory threshold ( T vent ), and used near‐infrared spectroscopy to determine tissue saturation index as a measure of skeletal muscle ( vastus lateralis ) oxygenation. Twelve participants cycled at cadences of 30, 50, 70, 90, and 110 revolutions per minute (rpm), each for 4 min, in a randomized sequence, interspersed with active recovery periods. Despite cardiopulmonary and metabolic responses being greater at 90% than at 70% T vent , and at 110 rpm compared with lower cadences, vastus lateralis oxygenation was not different between the two exercise intensities and five cadences tested. Our results indicate that skeletal muscle tissue saturation index is not substantially affected during cycling for short periods of time at constant, moderate exercise intensity at cadences between 30 and 110 rpm, suggesting that skeletal muscle oxygenation may not be an important negative feedback signal in the choice of self‐selected cadence during cycling at moderate exercise intensity. Introduction Despite bicycles allowing a wide choice of gears, self‐selected cadences are not necessarily the most energy efficient (Hansen et al. 2002 ; Whitty et al. 2009 ) particularly in noncyclists. A number of physiological, biomechanical, and psychological factors determine the selection of cadence, with exercise duration and intensity, energy cost, neuromuscular fatigue, joint moments, and comfort all having an effect (Takaishi et al. 1996 ; Marsh et al. 2000 ; Whitty et al. 2009 ). The factors, or interaction of factors responsible for the selection of cadence have been investigated extensively, but are not yet fully understood (Ansley and Cangley 2009 ; Vercruyssen and Brisswalter 2010 ). Cardiorespiratory responses may be important in the selection of cadence. Heart rate (HR), oxygen consumption ( V̇ O 2 ), carbon dioxide production ( V̇ CO 2 ), and ventilation ( V̇ E ) all increase with an increase in cadence (Hagberg et al. 1981 ; Hirano et al. 2015 ), either while cycling at moderate power outputs (Zoladz et al. 2000 ), or against no resistance (Tokui and Hirakoba 2007 ; Formenti et al. 2015 ). Afferent feedback signal from skeletal muscle oxygenation may also contribute to the selection of cadence (Amann et al. 2009 ; Richards et al. 2011 ). Near‐infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) allows real time, noninvasive investigation of skeletal muscle oxygenation, as measured by the tissue saturation index (TSI) during cycling. TSI provides an overall index of skeletal muscle oxygenation with oxyhemoglobin (OxyHb) and deoxyhemoglobin (HHb) considered indices of oxygen delivery and extraction, respectively (Grassi and Quaresima 2016 ). It is generally accepted that HHb increases and TSI decreases while cycling at increasing power output associated with increased metabolic rate (Takaishi et al. 2002b ; Ferreira et al. 2006 ; Boone et al. 2016 ). In contrast, TSI response to increased cadence at a fixed power output is less clear. For example, increasing cadence from 60 to 110 revolutions per minute (rpm) at a constant power output equivalent to 75% of the lactate threshold was associated with a decrease in mean TSI (Skovereng et al. 2016 , 2017 ), while in other studies increasing cadence from 40 to 80 rpm at a power output equivalent to 60% of the maximal oxygen consumption ( V̇ O 2max ) did not alter TSI (Kounalakis and Geladas 2012 ). An increase in cadence was associated with greater HHb (Skovereng et al. 2016 , 2017 ), no difference in HHb (Ferreira et al. 2006 ; Kounalakis and Geladas 2012 ; Zorgati et al. 2013 ), or reduced HHb (Zorgati et al. 2015 ). An increase in cadence was also associated with either greater OxyHb (Ferreira et al. 2006 ; Hirano et al. 2015 ), no difference in OxyHb (Zorgati et al. 2015 ), or reduced OxyHb (Kounalakis and Geladas 2012 ; Skovereng et al. 2016 ). These apparently contradictory findings may reflect differences in study design (e.g., exercise duration and effect of fatigue) and changes in blood volume, as indicated by total haemoglobin, which were not always reported in full. The aim of this study was, therefore, to investigate the effect of different pedaling cadences on vastus lateralis oxygenation and blood lactate concentration at exercise intensities below the ventilatory threshold (sub‐ T vent ) during cycling. We hypothesized that TSI would decrease both at a very low cadence (30 rpm) due to intermittent blood flow caused by the elevated intramuscular pressures, and at a high cadence (110 rpm) due to the associated increase in oxygen consumption.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of different cycling exercise intensities (70% and 90% of ventilatory threshold, Tvent) and cadences (30-110 rpm) on cardiopulmonary, metabolic, and skeletal muscle oxygenation responses in healthy participants. While higher intensity and cadence led to increased cardiorespiratory and metabolic activity, skeletal muscle oxygenation (measured by tissue saturation index and its oscillations) in the vastus lateralis was not substantially affected, suggesting it may not be a primary factor in self-selected cadence at moderate exercise intensity.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants performed cycling exercise at two intensities (70% and 90% of the ventilatory threshold, Tvent) and five cadences (30, 50, 70, 90, and 110 rpm), with each bout lasting 4 minutes in a randomized sequence, interspersed with active recovery. While cardiopulmonary and metabolic responses increased with higher intensity (90% Tvent) and higher cadences (especially 110 rpm), skeletal muscle oxygenation (TSI and its oscillations) in the vastus lateralis showed no significant dose-response across the tested intensities or cadences.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Tissue oxygenation index (measured via near-infrared spectroscopy)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification:
TSI was not different between 70% and 90% Tvent exercise intensities and across cadences (30-110 rpm). No significant difference in changes from baseline, with mean 
				TSI values averaging ~4% and not varying with intensity or cadence. Not substantially affected during short-duration cycling at moderate intensity.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Overall index of skeletal muscle oxygenation, reflecting the balance between oxygen delivery and extraction, and between oxygen supply and demand.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Cycling at moderate exercise intensities (70% and 90% Tvent) across various cadences (30-110 rpm) for short durations (4 min per cadence), with testing in randomized sequences and active recovery periods.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Suggests that skeletal muscle oxygenation is not an important negative feedback signal in the choice of self-selected cadence during cycling at moderate exercise intensity under these conditions.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification:
Approximately 20 bpm higher at 90% Tvent than at 70% Tvent (P < 0.05) across all cadences. At 110 rpm, HR (150 
						14 bpm at 70% Tvent; 166 
						10 bpm at 90% Tvent) was significantly higher compared to lower cadences (P < 0.002). Returned to resting levels after active recovery periods.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of cardiovascular effort, physiological strain, and workload, reflecting the body's response to oxygen demand during exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Cycling at different exercise intensities (70% vs 90% Tvent) and cadences (30-110 rpm), including post-active recovery periods.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates increased cardiovascular demand and exercise intensity with higher workload and cadences, with effective recovery between bouts.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification:

						1.16 mmol/L (70% Tvent) and 5.30

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Byproduct of anaerobic glycolysis, indicating metabolic stress, muscle fatigue, and the extent of anaerobic energy contribution.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Cycling at different exercise intensities (70% vs 90% Tvent) and cadences (30-110 rpm), particularly pronounced at 110 rpm during higher intensity.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of anaerobic metabolism, muscle fatigue onset, and exercise intensity approaching or exceeding the anaerobic threshold.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification:
Significantly greater at 90% Tvent than at 70% Tvent (except at the highest cadence, 110 rpm, where no difference was observed between intensities). Increased significantly at 110 rpm compared with 30, 50, 70, and 90 rpm (P < 0.001) at 70% Tvent. At 90% Tvent, V
				CO2 was significantly higher at 90 and 110 rpm compared with 70 rpm (P < 0.05).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects overall metabolic rate, fuel utilization, and the production of carbon dioxide as a result of cellular energy metabolism.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Cycling at different exercise intensities (70% vs 90% Tvent) and cadences (30-110 rpm).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of metabolic rate, physiological workload, and energy expenditure during exercise, showing an increase with higher intensity and cadence.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification:
Significantly greater at 90% Tvent compared to 70% Tvent (except at 110 rpm, where no difference was observed between intensities). Increased significantly at 110 rpm compared with 30, 50, 70, and 90 rpm (P < 0.001) at 70% Tvent. At 90% Tvent, V
				O2 was significantly higher at 90 and 110 rpm compared with 70 rpm (P < 0.05).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects the aerobic metabolic rate and the body's uptake of oxygen for energy production, indicating overall aerobic capacity and energy expenditure.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Cycling at different exercise intensities (70% vs 90% Tvent) and cadences (30-110 rpm).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicator of aerobic capacity, energy expenditure, and physiological workload during exercise, showing an increase with higher intensity and cadence.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Relative concentration change / Index of oxygen delivery

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: A significantly greater decrease from baseline was observed at 90% Tvent compared to 70% Tvent, specifically at cadences of 50 and 70 rpm (P < 0.05). Changes were not significantly different between various cadences.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Represents oxygen supply and utilization within the muscle, acting as an index of oxygen delivery to skeletal muscle.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Cycling at different exercise intensities (70% vs 90% Tvent) and cadences (30-110 rpm).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates reduced oxygen delivery to the muscle at higher exercise intensities, suggesting increased metabolic demand or potentially compromised supply.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Relative concentration change / Index of oxygen extraction

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant difference in changes from baseline for HHb between 70% and 90% Tvent, and not significantly different between various cadences.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Represents oxygen extraction by the muscle, reflecting the amount of hemoglobin that has released its oxygen, indicating muscle oxygen utilization status.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Cycling at different exercise intensities (70% vs 90% Tvent) and cadences (30-110 rpm).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates that oxygen extraction by the muscle is not significantly different across the tested exercise intensities and cadences under these conditions.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: TSI (Amplitude of Tissue Saturation Index Oscillation)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Not significantly different between 70% and 90% Tvent, and did not vary in response to changes in cadence. Values averaged approximately 4%.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Reflects dynamic changes in skeletal muscle oxygenation within each pedal revolution, potentially related to microvascular blood flow or oxygen extraction efficiency.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Cycling at different exercise intensities (70% vs 90% Tvent) and cadences (30-110 rpm).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potentially indicates the efficiency of muscle oxygen utilization and microcirculatory responses during dynamic exercise, but showed no significant variation in this study.
